messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Vulnerability: Being naked, Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Avoid Going Out: Going out, Avoid Exercise: Exercise
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh was 46 when he finally came to treatment, a married software engineer who had spent years trying to make his life look ordinary from the outside. The trauma he carried came from his time in combat, when he had been caught in a cramped, diesel-scented vehicle under fire and had learned in a matter of minutes that the body could be trapped, exposed, and helpless all at once. Even now, it was the smell that could take him back first: the sharp, oily odor of engines, hot metal, and sweat would catch him off guard in a parking garage or beside a passing motorcycle, and he would feel his chest tighten before he had time to think. The same was true of certain noises, especially the sudden mechanical burst of a motorcycle accelerating past the curb; in those moments he would be yanked into the old fear, and with it came the sense that danger was imminent. He had also come to dread nakedness in ordinary settings, not for any sexual reason but because being undressed made him feel exposed in exactly the way he had felt in the field, when there had been nowhere to hide.  

As those triggers began to accumulate in daily life, Minh quietly built his world around avoiding anything that might set them off. He stopped watching TV programmes or films about war, rescue missions, or attacks, and he would not read news stories that echoed his experience. He began turning down invitations to go out, especially to unfamiliar places, because he felt he could not assess the danger and did not trust himself to read a street, a crowd, or a room. Exercise, once a routine way of clearing his head, became something he avoided as well; getting his heart rate up made him feel too close to the bodily alarm he already lived with, and he preferred to stay still rather than invite that rush. At home, where his wife assumed he could relax, he remained on guard, scanning doors and windows and listening for noises outside, unable to settle even in his own living room. His job at the software company kept him at a desk, but it also gave him ways to hide: he could work late, skip social outings with colleagues, and keep his daily world narrow enough that fewer smells, strangers, and unpredictable places crossed his path.  

The problem was that the more he tried to keep certain things away, the more his mind seemed to give them back to him. Minh described his memories as a film that played over and over, and he could not seem to put the frightening event into words; when he tried, the story came out broken and thin, as if language could not hold what had happened. At times, when a smell or noise brought the memory close, he would hear pieces of it in his head exactly as they had sounded during the event, and those inner sounds made the scene feel even more immediate. Because he was avoiding anything that reminded him of combat, the memory never had a chance to feel ordinary or distant; instead it stayed vivid, replaying in fragments and images, returning without warning when he was least prepared. He found that after a week of staying indoors and skipping exercise, the memory seemed to press in more, not less, and even a brief look at a news clip or a motorcycle passing under his window could set the film running again.  

Minh’s sense of threat grew in parallel with this. He felt threatened by strangers approaching him even in ordinary situations, such as someone coming too close in a store aisle or walking up behind him in the apartment lobby, and his body reacted before he could reassure himself. He stayed vigilant inside his own home, and he had become wary of unfamiliar places because he could not assess what might happen there. At the same time, that constant watchfulness seemed to keep his mind circling back to the event: the more he scanned for danger, the more often the sounds and images returned, and the more his memories replayed, the more convinced he became that danger could appear anywhere. Smells from the street, the exposed feeling of being undressed after a shower, and the mechanical whine of a passing motorcycle all became potent because they matched pieces of what his threat system was already looking for. Over months, Minh’s attempts to avoid movies, going out, exercise, and other reminders brought short-term relief but also left him more isolated, more jumpy, and less able to tell himself that he was safe. He finally sought help after his wife noticed how far his world had shrunk and after a stranger approaching him near their building sent him into a panic so intense that he went home shaking, afraid that if he continued like this he would never feel secure again, and even more afraid that the war would keep living in his head forever.
